t: Product of Two Run-Length Encoded Arrays — Segment-by-Segment Two Pointers
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Two compressed arrays describe runs of repeated values: encoded1 expands to nums1 and encoded2 to nums2, and both full arrays share the same length L. The product is the run-length encoding (shortest possible) of the elementwise products prodNums[i] = nums1[i] * nums2[i].

**Walking through Example 1:** encoded1 = [[1,3],[2,3]] expands to [1,1,1,2,2,2] and encoded2 = [[6,3],[3,3]] to [6,6,6,3,3,3]. Elementwise products are [6,6,6,6,6,6]; compressing merges all six equal products into a single run [[6,6]].

**Example 2:** expansions are [1,1,1,2,3,3] and [2,2,2,3,3,3], so products are [2,2,2,6,9,9], which compress to [[2,3],[6,1],[9,2]].

**What the constraints imply:** with up to 10^5 segments per array and frequencies up to 10^4, the decompressed length can approach 10^9 — expanding explicitly would blow up time and memory. Instead we can walk both encodings in lockstep: two segments overlap for min(remaining frequency) positions, during which the product val1 * val2 is constant.
k: Never expand the arrays: overlapping prefixes of two segments produce a constant value v1 * v2 for exactly min(f1_remaining, f2_remaining) positions.
Consecutive equal products must merge into one run to satisfy the minimum-length compression requirement.
A two-pointer scan over segments does O(m + n) work regardless of how long the full arrays are.

a.i: The most literal implementation of the three-step definition: decompress both arrays, multiply position by position, then run-length encode the result by counting streaks of equal values. It is trivially correct and a fine reference model, but its cost scales with the decompressed length L, which reaches 10^5 segments * 10^4 frequency = 10^9 under the given limits — this will exceed time and memory limits on real tests.
s: Expand encoded1 into nums1 by repeating each value freq times; likewise encoded2 into nums2.
Build prodNums where prodNums[i] = nums1[i] * nums2[i].
Scan prodNums, starting a new run whenever the value changes from the previous element.
Return the list of [value, runLength] pairs.
a.t: O(L) where L is the decompressed length — up to 10^9 under these constraints, so it exceeds limits despite being linear in that length.
a.sp: O(L) — both expanded arrays are held in memory at once.

a.i: Keep one pointer per encoding plus each pointer's remaining frequency. At every step the current segments overlap for take = min(fi, fj) positions, all sharing the constant product val_i * val_j — append that run, or extend the previous output run if the product matches (this handles merging automatically). Subtract take from both remainders and advance whichever segment is exhausted. Total work depends only on segment counts, not on decompressed lengths.
s: Initialize i = j = 0 with fi = encoded1[0][1] and fj = encoded2[0][1].
While segments remain: take = min(fi, fj); prod = encoded1[i][0] * encoded2[j][0].
Append [prod, take] to the result, or add take to the last entry's frequency when its value equals prod.
Subtract take from fi and fj; when a remainder hits 0, advance that pointer and load its next frequency.
a.t: O(m + n) — each pointer advances once per segment, doing O(1) work per emitted run; independent of decompressed lengths.
a.sp: O(1) auxiliary — excluding the output, which holds at most m + n runs.

w: Go straight to Approach 2 after noting why expansion dies (L up to ~10^9); the lockstep-with-min-frequency pattern is the entire algorithm. Pitfalls: forgetting to merge adjacent equal products (Example 1 exists precisely to test this — three separate 6-runs would be rejected), off-by-one errors when a remainder hits zero inside the same iteration as an append, and assuming values can be negative — the stated constraints keep them positive, but the merge logic above works regardless. Edge cases: single-segment inputs whose products align into one giant run. Follow-ups: compute elementwise sum instead of product (same skeleton), handle arrays of different lengths, or implement division of two RLE arrays where exact alignment still guarantees integer quotients.
